We believe it is a good direction, and we believe we can continue to iterate it to a fully supportable and capable feature based upon feedback from ourselves and other users.  But as that feedback is collected and incorporated, we leave open the possibility that we may gain new knowledge and be required to change direction.

If you've used the plugin capability, please share any feedback to help build a case for us that it is worth committing to long-term support.  Any feedback on adjustments, tweaks, and adjustments needed is also welcome.  If you've experienced a specific bug, please create a new bug report for that so we can discuss it in detail and close it when it is fixed.

title: bug: Wrong PATH architecture in cross-platform Docker jobs
body:
### Can you reproduce the bug on the Forgejo test instance?

No

### Description

When running an AMD64 Docker job on an ARM host, the runner appears to reconstruct the job's PATH from the ARM variant of the image rather than the AMD64 variant that's actually executing the workflow.

After `actions/setup-python@v7`, for some reason PATH contains the ARM Node directory, despite the job container having the AMD64 Node installation.

This causes subsequent JavaScript actions to fail with `node: executable file not found in $PATH`.

I'm using the following label on a ARM host:

```yaml
runner:
  labels:
    - ubuntu-latest:docker://ghcr.io/catthehacker/ubuntu:act-24.04?platform=linux/amd64
```

Using this workflow:

```yaml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.14"

      - name: Debug PATH
        run: |
          echo "PATH=$PATH"
          command -v node || true
          node --version || true
          ls -l /opt/acttoolcache/node/24.19.0/x64/bin/node

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: "22"
```

The "Debug PATH" step prints:

```text
PATH=/opt/hostedtoolcache/Python/3.14.8/x64/bin:/opt/hostedtoolcache/Python/3.14.8/x64:/opt/acttoolcache/node/24.19.0/arm64/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/games:/usr/local/games:/snap/bin

/var/run/act/workflow/2.sh: line 4: node: command not found

-rwxr-xr-x 1 ubuntu ubuntu 125989464 Aug  3 07:53 /opt/acttoolcache/node/24.19.0/x64/bin/node
```

`actions/setup-node@v7` then fails:

```text
OCI runtime exec failed: exec failed: unable to start container process:
exec: "node": executable file not found in $PATH
```

However, directly launching the AMD64 image works:

```bash
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \
  --entrypoint node \
  ghcr.io/catthehacker/ubuntu:act-24.04 \
  --version
```

Output:

```text
v24.19.0
```

Inspecting the image **without specifying a platform** returns:

```bash
docker image inspect \
  ghcr.io/catthehacker/ubuntu:act-24.04 \
  --format '{{.Architecture}} {{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}' \
  | grep -E 'arm64|amd64|PATH='
```

Output:

```text
arm64 DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
PATH=/opt/acttoolcache/node/24.19.0/arm64/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/games:/usr/local/games:/snap/bin
```

This PATH matches the incorrect one appearing in the AMD64 job after Python setup.


The workaround I've been using is to explicitly restore the AMD64 Node directory after `setup-python`:

```yaml
- name: Restore Node runtime PATH
  run: |
    echo "/opt/acttoolcache/node/24.19.0/x64/bin" >> "$FORGEJO_PATH"
```

I was not able to reproduce this bug in the Forgejo test instance due to the specific condition that the test runner must have an ARM Docker daemon executing an AMD64 job image, and it seems like the test instance has no runners at all.

### Forgejo Version

v15.0.9

### Runner Version

v13.2.0

### How are you running Forgejo?

Docker container

### How are you running the Runner?

Docker container

### Logs

See description

### Workflow file

See description

title: bug: runner.fetch_interval is ignored when registered via .runner (v13.2.0); honored under server.connections
body:
### Can you reproduce the bug on the Forgejo test instance?

No

### Description

## Observed
With a runner registered via `forgejo-runner register` (credentials in `.runner`) and this in `config.yml`:

    runner:
      fetch_interval: 20s

the daemon (`forgejo-runner daemon --config config.yml`) still sends `RunnerService/FetchTask` every 2 s.

Proved by request timestamps from `tcpdump` on loopback (HTTP, 30 s capture): 15 requests, constant 2.000 s step. 14 `FetchTask` POSTs counted in another 30 s capture.

The config file itself is being read (e.g. `log.level` and `container.options` take effect).

## Effect
Idle Forgejo (server) process CPU, averaged over 60 s from cgroup `cpu.stat`:
- runner stopped: Forgejo **0.47%** of one core
- runner running with default config: Forgejo **1.43%**
- runner running, `fetch_interval: 20s` / `report_interval: 10s` under `runner:`: Forgejo **1.47%**

##  Workaround that worked
Moved `.runner` away and described the connection in `config.yml` instead:

    server:
      connections:
        local:
          url: http://127.0.0.1:3680/
          uuid: <uuid from .runner>
          token_url: file:/data/token.txt
          fetch_interval: 20s
          labels:
            - nix:docker://nixos/nix

With this the runner declares itself normally and Forgejo idle CPU dropped to ~0.3% with short bursts roughly every 20 s (observed in CPU usage; I did not re-count requests).

BTW, I had to move `.runner`, because if `.runner` is left in place alongside `server.connections`, the daemon exits with: `invalid configuration: server connection conflict between ".runner" and config; only one config file can provide server connections`.

## Note

FYI. No action requested. Did not try to reproduce on  https://dev.next.forgejo.org.

16.0.5

v13.2.0

Rootless podman (codeberg.org/orbit/orbit:16.0.5-rootless)

title: bug: lookup/download race in artifact cache
body:
### Can you reproduce the bug on the Forgejo test instance?

No

### Description

(Note: I can repro in a test against latest main `7917d26c75dc9ca77aeb0c319b0afc314deaf2f7`.)

behold, a CI failure, 404 in the artifact cache.

```
::error::buildx bake failed with: ERROR: target task-full: failed to solve: failed to compute cache key: failed to copy: invalid status response 404 Not Found for http://10.0.5.204:41089/b405c6c0fb596bc11ad0b86b42c22b83/_apis/artifactcache/artifacts/2092
```

I believe that this is caused by a race between `GET /cache` and `GET /artifacts/:id`. seems that in some circumstances the GC can delete the artifact in the URL that `GET /cache` just returned, maybe even as part of the same request. In my logs  `GET /artifacts/:id` is called around 5 seconds after `GET /cache`

I believe the artifact cache has a "useCache" function which can prevent the artifact from being GC'd for a short time in some cases. To me it makes sense to use that functionality for the artifact URL returned by `GET /cache` to help mitigate this race.

title: Deprecation Cleanup for Major Release v14
bug: `timeout-minutes` kill breaks post-step Runner File Command extraction - "context deadline exceeded"
body:
### Can you reproduce the bug on the Forgejo test instance?

No

### Description

When a job hits its own `timeout-miutes`, the "Runner File Command" tail (reads `SUMMARY.md`, `pathcmd.txt`, `envs.txt`, `outputcmd.txt`, `statecmd.txt` from the container) that runs after every step runs on the _same_ context that the timeout just killed.

All calls fail without a real request going on.

```
⚙️ [runner]: context deadline exceeded
unable to copy "/var/run/act/workflow/SUMMARY.md" from container to host: Get "http://%2Fvar%2Frun%2Fpodman%2Fpodman.sock/v1.44/containers/…/archive?path=%2Fvar%2Frun%2Fact%2Fworkflow%2FSUMMARY.md": context deadline exceeded
unable to copy "/var/run/act/workflow/pathcmd.txt" from container to host: Get "http://%2Fvar%2Frun%2Fpodman%2Fpodman.sock/v1.44/containers/…/archive?path=%2Fvar%2Frun%2Fact%2Fworkflow%2Fpathcmd.txt": context deadline exceeded
```

1. The Job-level `timeout-minutes` wraps the whole job executor: [`act/runner/run_context.go#L1143-L1146`](https://code.forgejo.org/orbit/orbit/src/tag/v13.0.0/act/runner/run_context.go#L1143-L1146)
```go
if timeoutMinutes != nil {
    common.Logger(ctx).Debugf("The job will stop in %d minutes", *timeoutMinutes)
    ctx, cancelFunc = context.WithTimeout(ctx, time.Duration(*timeoutMinutes)*time.Minute)
}
```

2. Step-level `timeout-minutes` does the _same_ thing but one level down.: [`act/runner/step.go#L191-L194`](https://code.forgejo.org/orbit/orbit/src/tag/v13.0.0/act/runner/step.go#L191-L194)
```go
if timeoutMinutes != nil {
    common.Logger(ctx).Debugf("The step will stop in %d minutes", *timeoutMinutes)
    ctx, cancelFunc = context.WithTimeout(ctx, time.Duration(*timeoutMinutes)*time.Minute)
}
```
This one is the actually broken part. This breaks even when the whole job still has plenty of time left. Nothing about one step's deadline should stop us from reading the step's own summary file.

3. Right after `executor(ctx)` return (same `ctx` from one of the two above or neither), the tail that reads the 5 files run unconditionally: [`act/runner/step.go#L221-L227`](https://code.forgejo.org/orbit/orbit/src/tag/v13.0.0/act/runner/step.go#L221-L227)
```go
// Process Runner File Commands
ferrors := []error{err}
ferrors = append(ferrors, processRunnerEnvFileCommand(ctx, envFileCommand, rc, rc.setEnv))
ferrors = append(ferrors, processRunnerEnvFileCommand(ctx, stateFileCommand, rc, rc.saveState))
ferrors = append(ferrors, processRunnerEnvFileCommand(ctx, outputFileCommand, rc, rc.setOutput))
ferrors = append(ferrors, processRunnerSummaryCommand(ctx, summaryFileCommand, rc))
ferrors = append(ferrors, rc.UpdateExtraPath(ctx, path.Join(actPath, pathFileCommand)))
return errors.Join(ferrors...)
```

4. `GetContainerArchive` forwards whatever ctx it gets with no timeout of its own: [`act/container/docker/run.go#L199-L207`](https://code.forgejo.org/orbit/orbit/src/tag/v13.0.0/act/container/docker/run.go#L199-L207)
```go
func (cr *containerReference) GetContainerArchive(ctx context.Context, srcPath string) (io.ReadCloser, error) {
    if common.Dryrun(ctx) {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("DRYRUN is not supported in GetContainerArchive")
    }
    result, err := cr.cli.CopyFromContainer(ctx, cr.id, client.CopyFromContainerOptions{SourcePath: srcPath})
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("unable to copy %q from container to host: %w", srcPath, err)
    }
    return result.Content, nil
}
```

When the ctx is already expired here then the docker client fails this instantly. No request happens at all.

5. Only 2 of the 5 show up in the log: the 3 that go through `ParseEnvFile` swallow the error and just return `nil` instead of propagating it.

[`act/container/parse_env_file.go#L17-L23`](https://code.forgejo.org/orbit/orbit/src/tag/v13.0.0/act/container/parse_env_file.go#L17-L23)
```go
func ParseEnvFile(e Container, srcPath string, env *map[string]string) common.Executor {
    localEnv := *env
    return func(ctx context.Context) error {
        envTar, err := e.GetContainerArchive(ctx, srcPath)
        if err != nil {
            return nil
        }
```

So on a timeout the `GITHUB_ENV` / `GITHUB_OUTPUT` / `GITHUB_STATE` get dropped without any diagnostic at all.
Only SUMMARY.md and the extra-PATH file show the error.

Maybe there should be a short-lived context for the cleanup read instead of reusing the dead one.
Also it would probably be good to make `ParseEnvFile` stop swallowing the error silently. :wink:

### Forgejo Version

v16.0.2

### Runner Version

v13.0.0

### How are you running Forgejo?

As Podman container

As Podman container

on: workflow_dispatch
jobs:

title: feat(plugin): cleanup/reconcilation of orphaned/lost environments
body:
If a runner->plugin interaction with `Create`/`Start` is not followed by a `Remove`, then the environment will be left on the system, consuming resources indefinitely.  This could happen for any number of reasons, such as a process crash.

Proposed design:
- The runner sends a unique identifier for the runner to `Create`, indicating the identity of the runner.  The plugin optionally records that identifier and associates it with the environment being created.
- Intermittently, the runner will take an inventory of the environments that it knows exists within a plugin.  Then, it will send a new command to the runner, `Inventory(RunnerID string, EnvironmentIDs []string)`.
- The plugin will be capable of inventorying the system, and finding all the existing environments that have the runner ID associated with them.  If an environment exists, but it is not in the environment list, the plugin can recognize that it is an orphaned environment.
- The plugin can then perform a cleanup.

Through this process, no matter what process crashes occur between the runner and the plugin, the plugin will always be able to identify orphaned resources (even that were lost in memory) and clean them up.  The unique RunnerID is used in order to allow one plugin instance to be shared between multiple runners, but may be a complication that isn't necessary.

(cc: @maya2 -- don't take this as a request to implement this immediately, but just a note about the problem -- I'm documenting a few of the issues I discovered while building a plugin implementation.)

title: chore(plugin): `CopyOut` is difficult to author for a plugin creator
body:
- It seems to actually be used for files, seemingly only for single files?, to read the env files.  But the API is that we're returning a tar file stream which implies it will be used for directories.
- The tar file returned cannot actually be a directory -- e.g. if you tar up a directory with a single file in it, the tar will generate a header with metadata about the directory, and the runner will treat that metadata header as the env file.  It must be a tar file with a single file in it.

Perhaps, if the only needed capability at this time is to fetch a single file, a single file fetch routine would be easier to author rather than having to create a tarfile for no reason.  If both are needed, then Forgejo should be more accepting of tarfiles and look for the file it wants in the tarfile.

(cc: @maya2 -- don't take this as a request to fix this immediately, but just a note about the problem -- I'm documenting a few of the issues I discovered while building a plugin implementation.)
